issues.legal_issue: A High Court does not vitiate its decision in an income-tax reference by relying on facts admitted by the parties or found by the income-tax authorities.
material_facts: The High Court relied on facts admitted between the parties or found by the income-tax authorities.
The Revenue contended that the High Court had reappraised the facts and therefore its finding was vitiated.
issues.conclusion: The contention was without substance because the High Court relied on admitted or previously found facts, and its finding was not vitiated.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal from a decision on an income-tax reference under section 66A(2) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922, a finding is not vitiated where the High Court relies on facts admitted between the parties or found by the income-tax authorities; no earlier case was cited on this point.

predicates.income_tax_reference_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a High Court's decision on an income-tax reference.
predicates.high_court_relied_on_admitted_or_found_f: The High Court relied on facts admitted by the parties or found by the income-tax authorities.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a High Court's decision on an income-tax reference and the High Court relied on admitted or previously found facts, its finding is not vitiated.

issues.legal_issue: Expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred for business that is not capital in nature may qualify for deduction as business expenditure even if repairs are not current repairs.
material_facts: The assessee claimed a deduction for expenditure on renovating buildings, reconditioning machinery and clearing accumulated debris so that mining operations could resume.
The expenditure was incurred wholly and exclusively for the business.
The Revenue argued that the expenditure could not be considered under the residuary business-expenditure provision because the work was not current repairs.
issues.conclusion: Even if the expenditure did not constitute current repairs, it could be considered for deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(v) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922, concerns current repairs; it does not declare or necessarily imply that other repairs cannot qualify under section 10(2)(xv). The latter provision should be construed liberally, consistently with the commercial principle that business expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred for business and not capital in nature is deducted in computing profits. The Court relied on C.I.T. v. Chitnis, Motipur Sugar Factory Ltd. v. C.I.T., Devi Films Ltd. v. C.I.T., Badridas Daga v. C.I.T., Calcutta Co. Ltd. v. C.I.T., and The Law Shipping Co. Ltd. v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue.

rule.if: business_income_deduction_claim and expenditure_wholly_for_business and expenditure_not_capital and (repairs_are_current or repairs_are_not_current)

predicates.business_income_deduction_claim: A taxpayer claims a deduction for expenditure in computing income from a business.
predicates.expenditure_wholly_for_business: The taxpayer incurred the expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business.
predicates.expenditure_not_capital: The expenditure is not capital in nature.
predicates.repairs_are_current: The claimed expenditure is for repairs that qualify as current repairs.
predicates.repairs_are_not_current: The claimed expenditure is for repairs that do not qualify as current repairs.

issues.definition: A business deduction may be allowed where the taxpayer claims it for expenditure wholly incurred for business and the expenditure is not capital in nature, whether or not the repairs are current repairs.

issues.legal_issue: Expenditure to restore a temporarily suspended operating unit of an existing business is revenue expenditure when it creates no new asset or enduring business advantage.
material_facts: The assessee carried on coal-mining through a network of collieries, and the business continued while one colliery was temporarily unable to operate because it had been requisitioned for military use.
The assessee incurred expenditure to renovate the buildings, recondition the machinery and remove accumulated debris to resume mining operations after the colliery was returned.
No new asset was brought into existence and no enduring advantage for the business was acquired.
The colliery had been treated as an asset of the continuing business during its occupation, and expenditure incurred for it during that period had been allowed as business expenditure.
issues.conclusion: The expenditure was revenue in character and not capital expenditure.
issues.legal_principle: Whether expenditure is capital or revenue is determined by applying relevant tests in light of the particular facts. Under the tests referred to in Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. C.I.T., restoration of an existing business unit after a temporary suspension, without creating a new asset or acquiring an enduring business advantage, is revenue expenditure when incurred as part of the profit-earning process.

rule.if: business_income_deduction_claim and business_operates_through_multiple_units and one_unit_temporarily_suspended and restoration_work_resumes_existing_operations and no_new_asset_created and no_enduring_business_advantage_acquired

predicates.business_income_deduction_claim: A taxpayer claims a deduction for expenditure in computing income from a business.
predicates.business_operates_through_multiple_units: The business is carried on through multiple operating units.
predicates.one_unit_temporarily_suspended: One operating unit's activity was temporarily suspended while the business continued through other units.
predicates.restoration_work_resumes_existing_operat: The expenditure was incurred to restore an existing unit so that its established operations could resume.
predicates.no_new_asset_created: The restoration work brought no new asset into existence.
predicates.no_enduring_business_advantage_acquired: The expenditure acquired no enduring advantage for the business.

issues.definition: Expenditure claimed as a business deduction is revenue rather than capital when it restores a temporarily suspended unit of a continuing multi-unit business, resumes existing operations, and creates neither a new asset nor an enduring business advantage.
